density-fluids-s1.title: Four metal samples
density-fluids-s1.text: A student measures the mass of four small metal samples on a balance and finds each volume by lowering the sample into a graduated cylinder of water and reading the rise in the water level.

table.caption: Mass and volume of each sample

density-fluids-s2.title: Squeezing a syringe
density-fluids-s2.text:
Two identical sealed syringes have their tips blocked. Syringe 1 holds 20 cm³ of air; syringe 2 holds 20 cm³ of water. A student pushes each plunger with the same force.

The plunger of syringe 1 moves in noticeably and springs back when released. The plunger of syringe 2 hardly moves at all.

items.q: What is the density of sample B in SI units? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: 8.96 is the density in g/cm³. Convert: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
Value: you divided volume by mass. Density is mass per volume, ρ = m/V.

why.correct: ρ = m/V = 89.6 g / 10.0 cm³ = 8.96 g/cm³. Since 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³), ρ = 8.96 × 10³ kg/m³.

items.q: Which two samples could be made of the same metal?
options: A and C
A and B
B and D
C and D

why.correct: Density is a property of the material, not of the sample's size. A: 27.0/10.0 = 2.70 g/cm³; C: 54.0/20.0 = 2.70 g/cm³. Same density, likely the same metal (aluminum has 2.70 g/cm³).
options: Right: C has twice the mass and twice the volume of A, so the same density.
A has 2.70 g/cm³ and B has 8.96 g/cm³: same volume, very different masses.
B has 8.96 g/cm³ and D has 19.3 g/cm³.
C has 2.70 g/cm³ and D has 19.3 g/cm³; D's small volume makes its mass misleading.

items.q: Sample C is cut into two pieces, one twice the volume of the other. How does the density of the smaller piece compare with the density of sample C?
options: It is the same
It is one third as large
It is half as large
It is two thirds as large

why.correct: Cutting reduces mass and volume in the same ratio, so m/V does not change. Density belongs to the material.
options: Right: density does not depend on how much of the material you have.
The smaller piece has one third of the mass and one third of the volume, so the ratio is unchanged.
Halving would need the mass to drop without the volume dropping.
Both mass and volume shrink by the same factor.

items.q: A block of the same metal as sample D has a volume of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. What is its mass? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used 19.3 g/cm³ with a volume in m³. Convert the density first: 19.3 g/cm³ = 1.93 × 10⁴ kg/m³.
Value: you divided the volume by the density. m = ρV.

items.q: What does the experiment show about the two fluids?
options: Water is nearly incompressible; air is easily compressed
Both fluids are incompressible, since neither leaks out
The air is nearly incompressible, but the water is compressed
Neither is a fluid, because they are trapped in the syringe

why.correct: Squeezing changed the air's volume noticeably but not the water's. Liquids are close to incompressible because their particles are already touching; gas particles are far apart.
options: Right: water's volume hardly changes under the push.
Not leaking does not make a fluid incompressible; the air's volume clearly shrank.
This reverses the observations: the air plunger moved in.
A fluid is defined by flowing and taking its container's shape, which both do.

items.q: What happens to the density of the air in syringe 1 while the plunger is pushed in?
options: It increases, because the same mass occupies a smaller volume
It stays the same, because no air leaves the syringe
It decreases, because the particles are pushed apart
It stays the same, because density is a property of the material

why.correct: The blocked tip keeps the mass of air fixed, while the volume shrinks. ρ = m/V, so the density rises. A compressible fluid's density can change.
options: Right: same m, smaller V, larger ρ.
The mass stays the same, but density is mass per volume and the volume shrank.
Pushing the plunger in squeezes the particles closer together, not farther apart.
For an incompressible fluid density is fixed, but air is compressible.

items.q: When fluids are treated as ideal on the exam, which property is assumed?
options: Its density stays the same as it flows and is squeezed
The fluid sticks to the walls of its container
The fluid has no mass, so it exerts no forces
The fluid keeps its shape when it is poured

why.correct: An ideal fluid is incompressible (constant density) and nonviscous (no internal friction), and its flow is smooth and steady.
options: Right: incompressible means constant density.
Sticking to walls is a sign of viscosity, which an ideal fluid lacks.
An ideal fluid has mass and weight; only its friction is ignored.
No fluid keeps its shape; that is the difference between a fluid and a solid.

items.q: Why is liquid water much harder to compress than air?
options: Water particles already touch; air particles are far apart
Water particles are locked in fixed places, as in a solid
Water has a larger mass than air, so it is harder to move
Air particles attract each other more strongly than water particles do

why.correct: In a liquid the particles touch and slide past each other; there is little empty space to squeeze out. In a gas most of the volume is empty space between particles.
options: Right: the spacing of the particles decides how compressible the fluid is.
Water particles can slide past each other; that is why water flows.
The two syringes hold the same volume; the difference is in particle spacing, not mass.
In a gas the attractions between particles are weak, which is why they spread out.

items.q: Which of these is a fluid?
options: Honey
A steel ball bearing
A block of ice
A rubber band

why.correct: A fluid is a substance that flows and takes the shape of its container: a liquid or a gas. Honey flows, slowly.
options: Right: honey is a liquid, so it is a fluid (a viscous one).
Steel keeps its own shape: a solid.
Ice is solid water; it keeps its shape until it melts.
A rubber band can stretch but keeps a shape of its own; it does not flow.

items.q: A rectangular swimming pool is 10.0 m long, 5.0 m wide and filled to a depth of 2.0 m with water of density 1000 kg/m³. What is the mass of the water? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the weight in newtons (you multiplied by g). The question asks for the mass, m = ρV.
Value: you added the dimensions. Volume is length × width × depth.

why.correct: V = 10.0 m × 5.0 m × 2.0 m = 100 m³. m = ρV = (1000 kg/m³)(100 m³) = 1.0 × 10⁵ kg, about 100 metric tons.

items.q: Cube X is made of the same material as cube Y but has sides twice as long. How does the mass of X compare with the mass of Y?
options: 8 times as large
2 times as large
4 times as large
The same

why.correct: Same material, same density. Volume = side³, so doubling the side gives 2³ = 8 times the volume, and m = ρV gives 8 times the mass.
options: Right: volume, and so mass, goes as the cube of the side.
This treats the volume as proportional to the side length.
This uses the area of one face (side²) instead of the volume.
Density is the same, but a bigger cube contains more material.

items.q: A sealed bottle of air is warmed in the sun, and its volume does not change. What happens to the density of the air inside?
options: It stays the same, because m and V do not change
It increases, because the particles move faster
It decreases, because warm air is less dense
It increases, because the pressure inside rises

why.correct: ρ = m/V. The bottle is sealed (same mass) and rigid (same volume), so the density is unchanged even though the particles move faster.
options: Right: density depends only on mass and volume.
Faster particles raise the pressure, not the mass or volume.
Warm air is less dense only when it is free to expand; this bottle is sealed and rigid.
The pressure does rise, but density is mass per volume, which has not changed.

items.q: A 250 cm³ sample of olive oil has a mass of 0.229 kg. What is its density in SI units? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the volume in cm³ with a mass in kg. Convert: 250 cm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Value: 250 cm³ is 0.250 L, not 0.250 m³. 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, so 250 cm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

why.correct: V = 250 cm³ = 250 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³. ρ = m/V = 0.229 kg / 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 916 kg/m³, a little less than water.

items.q: A brick is weighed, then sawn into two halves. Predict how each quantity for one half compares with the whole brick.

variables.name: Mass
variables.why: Half the material, so half the mass.

variables.name: Volume
variables.why: Half the material takes up half the space.

variables.name: Density
variables.why: Mass and volume both halve, so their ratio ρ = m/V does not change.

why.correct: Density is a property of the material; mass and volume depend on how much material there is.

items.q: What makes a liquid different from a solid at the level of its particles?
options: The particles can slide past one another, so it flows
The particles are much farther apart, so the liquid is easy to compress
The particles do not attract each other
The particles stop moving when the liquid is at rest

why.correct: In both solids and liquids the particles are close together, but in a liquid they are not locked in place, so the liquid flows.
options: Right: particles that slide past each other make a fluid.
Particles far apart describe a gas; liquids are nearly incompressible.
Liquid particles attract each other; that is what holds a drop together.
The particles keep moving even when the liquid as a whole is still.
